interior.title: Cognition · the interior sentence
interior.text: Many leaders are one bad interior sentence away from a quarter of poor decisions: the silent conclusion that the situation is unwinnable or that the board has already decided. Write down the sentence running in your head about the future, and test it against the evidence.

significance.title: Emotion · significance
significance.text: Organisations that reduce everything to deliverables and KPIs, with no sense of what it is all for, produce people who show up physically and are absent in every other way. People need to feel the significance of what they are part of.

why.title: Principle 1 · explain the why
why.text: Leaders who consistently explain the why behind hard decisions, structural changes and accountability moments build a culture of understanding. Every significant leadership act should leave people knowing something true about the organisation’s direction and character.

continuous.title: Chinese Whispers · continuous direction
continuous.text: Organisations that communicate direction only in crisis moments find that the alignment achieved has dissipated by the next one. Consistent, continuous direction communication produces lasting alignment.

receiver.title: Clarification Debt · designed for the receiver
receiver.text: Leadership communication must be designed for the receiver. Expertise becomes ineffective when it cannot be translated into clear understanding.

knowledgegap.title: Leaders own the knowledge gap
knowledgegap.text: Where people do not know the governing principles, the strategic direction or the cultural standards, drift follows. The leaders responsible for communicating them are accountable for the gap between what people know and what they need to know.

certainty.title: Certainty · unfamiliar territory
certainty.text: In unfamiliar territory, address the fear in the team directly, promise presence and support, and describe what success looks like and how the team will know it has been achieved.

legitimacy.title: Resistance and legitimacy
legitimacy.text: Leaders who answer resistance with escalating force are solving for control when the problem is legitimacy. Ask why the resistance exists before deciding how to respond.

obstacle.title: Resistance as information
obstacle.text: Repeated resistance can be the signal of a genuine obstacle. Leaders who suppress it without investigating its source risk striking the messenger and missing the obstacle.

integrity.title: Integrity · practice and statement
integrity.text: The team reads the practice and discounts the statement, and the gap between the two is where credibility erodes fastest. Name where your stated position and your lived practice run in opposite directions, and close the gap before someone else names it.

committing.title: Knowing and committing
committing.text: Strategic paralysis often comes from the gap between knowing what needs to happen and committing to do it. If the strategy has been articulated and nothing has moved in a quarter, the bottleneck is the commitment.

conviction.title: Conduct and conviction
conviction.text: A leader can manage someone’s conduct without ever securing their conviction. Ask this about the people you are developing: do they understand why well enough to sustain it without me? Dependence on the leader’s presence is managed behaviour.

understood.title: Published and understood
understood.text: Organisations often assume that completing a restructure, implementing a system or publishing a strategy means transformation has occurred. Sustainable results require people to understand what the change means, why it matters and what they must now do differently.

adoption.title: Engagement without adoption
adoption.text: A draining pattern in mature teams is engagement without adoption: the team attends, questions and challenges, and the decision is never received. Name the pattern directly, then either revise the decision or close the debate and call for adoption.

strain.title: Listening to strain
strain.text: A strategy that cannot absorb honest feedback becomes disconnected from reality. When operational strain, excessive demands or declining trust are raised, assess how people are experiencing the system. Early listening is the intervention that stabilises a High Flammable Zone.

soil.title: Diagnose the soil
soil.text: The same input lands differently depending on the ground it falls on. When a change initiative fails to take, the reflex is to blame the message. First diagnose the conditions stopping good input from rooting.

whole.title: Distinct contribution, shared whole
whole.text: Healthy cultures value distinct contribution and collaboration together. They discourage empire-building and needless overlap, and help people strengthen the whole through clear roles and mutual support.

listening.title: Listening first
listening.text: Teams that move straight from ‘here is what changed’ to ‘here is what we need you to do next’ produce resistance they cannot explain. The resistance signals that people do not yet feel understood.

openq.title: One open question
openq.text: Pressure and assumption turn silence into disengagement and intensity into instability. Before correcting, ask one open question, ‘What’s going on for you today?’, and wait for the answer.
